title: Autoimmune Bullous Disease — Treatment Ladder
subtitle: By disease and phase of therapy: induction → maintenance → adjunct/refractory

induction.text: Rituximab plus a short prednisone course for appropriate moderate–severe pemphigus
induction.detail: Ritux 3 (Joly 2017) compared rituximab plus short prednisone with prednisone alone. The rituximab arm used 1 g on days 0 and 14, 500 mg at months 12 and 18, and prednisone 0.5 or 1 mg/kg/day tapered over 3 or 6 months according to severity. This is not the later PEMPHIX rituximab-versus-mycophenolate trial. Individualize labeled treatment and screening.

maintenance.text: Clinical reassessment and individualized maintenance / relapse treatment
maintenance.detail: Maintenance doses were already included at months 12 and 18 in Ritux 3. Subsequent treatment follows the current label and guideline, disease activity, infection risk and immunoglobulin status. An antibody rise alone does not mandate re-treatment; use clinical assessment.

adjunct.text: Specialist options for refractory pemphigus; investigational agents are not standard therapy
adjunct.detail: Re-evaluate diagnosis, adherence, infection and prior regimen before escalation. IVIG or immunoadsorption may have selected roles. Do not infer efficacy of an investigational FcRn or CD40L agent from a general 2019 review; agent-specific trial results are required.

induction.text: Prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day (lower dose than PV — no mucosal disease); rituximab if moderate–severe
induction.detail: PF without mucosal involvement generally responds to lower-dose systemic steroids than PV. Prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day initiated with early steroid-sparing agent. Rituximab 1 g ×2 is effective for moderate–severe PF and recommended for refractory disease. Dapsone 50–150 mg may control limited superficial PF. Anti-Dsg1 ELISA guides response.

maintenance.text: Taper prednisone; MMF 2–3 g/day or azathioprine as steroid-sparing; dapsone for limited stable disease
maintenance.detail: Steroid taper similar to PV. MMF (mycophenolate mofetil) 2–3 g/day is preferred steroid-sparing agent in many centers. Dapsone 50–150 mg can maintain remission in limited superficial PF. Monitor anti-Dsg1 titers; rising titer + new lesions indicates relapse. Fogo selvagem endemic variant may require long-term low-dose maintenance.

adjunct.text: Specialist re-evaluation and evidence-based pemphigus options
adjunct.detail: Moderate–severe or refractory PF may warrant rituximab and other systemic options with disease-specific evidence. The previous routine hydroxychloroquine recommendation was not supported by the cited guideline and is not retained as an established treatment.

induction.text: Superpotent topical corticosteroid when practical; systemic options individualized
induction.detail: The 2002 trial used clobetasol 40 g/day initially. In extensive BP, one-year survival was 76% with topical treatment versus 58% with oral prednisone—not mortality of 41% versus 58%. Dose, area and taper require supervision because systemic absorption occurs. Doxycycline evidence does not establish that adding niacinamide reproduces the trial regimen.

maintenance.text: Taper topical clobetasol over 12 months; add MMF or methotrexate for extensive or relapsing disease
maintenance.detail:
Taper schedule: after initial 4-week induction at full dose, reduce clobetasol frequency and area over 12 months. Anti-BP180 ELISA titer guides tapering — rising titer predicts relapse.

MMF 2–3 g/day or methotrexate 5–15 mg/week as steroid-sparing adjuncts for extensive BP or patients requiring prolonged topical steroids (skin atrophy, adrenal suppression risk). Doxycycline 100–200 mg/day as maintenance for patients who responded to doxycycline induction. PMID: 35743598.

adjunct.text: Dupilumab is US-approved for adult BP; other agents have different evidence and labeling
adjunct.detail: The adult BP label specifies dupilumab 600 mg initially, then 300 mg every two weeks with a tapering oral-corticosteroid course; after disease control it may continue alone. Omalizumab and rituximab have different, off-label BP evidence and should not be presented as equivalent approved options.

induction.text: Risk-stratify by involved mucosal sites and threat of scarring or functional loss
induction.detail: Ocular, laryngeal, esophageal and other function-threatening involvement requires prompt multidisciplinary management. Systemic regimens depend on severity and patient factors. The former generic 2 g/m² IV cyclophosphamide instruction was not supported by the cited source and has been removed; use a disease-specific specialist protocol.

maintenance.text: Long-term steroid-sparing immunosuppression; ophthalmology and ENT co-management; monitor for new mucosal sites
maintenance.detail:
After cyclophosphamide induction (ocular severe): switch to MMF 2–3 g/day or azathioprine once remission achieved. Duration of treatment: often years; MMP tends to be chronic and slowly progressive.

Monitor: periodic slit-lamp exam (ophthalmology) for conjunctival scarring progression. Nasal endoscopy (ENT) if nasopharyngeal involvement. Esophageal involvement: periodic dilation if dysphagia + stricture. Dental involvement: specialist dental care to prevent tooth loss. PMID: 35743598.

adjunct.text: Refractory disease and cicatricial sequelae need specialist management
adjunct.detail: Confirm anti-laminin 332 with specific testing, not routine DIF pattern alone. Associated malignancy warrants individualized assessment; the former universal CT/colonoscopy/gynecologic testing annually for two years was not established by the cited evidence. Procedures require control of inflammation and site-specific expertise.

induction.text: Dapsone for rapid symptom control plus a gluten-free diet after diagnostic assessment
induction.detail: A rapid dapsone response is not specific for DH. Check G6PD, CBC and relevant baseline safety studies. Monitor blood counts closely early and thereafter under the product and local protocol; a single two-week check followed by three-month intervals is insufficient as a universal schedule. Dapsone does not treat gluten-sensitive enteropathy.

maintenance.text: Dietitian-supported gluten-free diet; reduce dapsone as disease control permits
maintenance.detail: Monitor symptoms, nutrition and relevant celiac markers. Histologic recovery and reduction in medication requirement vary; neither antibody normalization nor diet adherence guarantees elimination of malignancy risk.

adjunct.text: Sulfapyridine 500–2000 mg/day if dapsone intolerant; sulfamethoxypyridazine (colchicine rarely used); nutritional supplementation
adjunct.detail:
Sulfapyridine 500–2000 mg/day: alternative if dapsone not tolerated (G6PD deficiency, severe anemia, agranulocytosis, dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome). Less effective than dapsone but well-tolerated. Adequate fluid intake to prevent crystalluria.

Sulfamethoxypyridazine (not available in all countries): another alternative.

Nutritional supplements: Iron, folate, vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium — supplement for malabsorption from celiac enteropathy. Monitor bone density (DXA).

Oats: Controversy — uncontaminated oats tolerated by most DH/celiac patients but avoid initially. PMID: 35743598.
